text: She got it, in 1876.
India gave Britain smaller things, too.
In 1814, an Indian businessman opened a bathhouse in Brighton,
offering a head massage called chumpo.
Today, you'd call it shampoo.
Under the Raj, India got railways.
Remember those bricks from Harappa?
Same railway age.
The tracks ran mainly to carry raw cotton to the ports,
and British factory cloth back in. Think about that. India, the land of Calico and
Chintz, the land that once dressed half the world, now bought its cloth from
Manchester. And the famines kept coming. In the great famine of 1876, millions
died while grain was still being exported. Then an Indian thinker named
Daddabai Naoroji sat down with the numbers.
Remember Pliny, the Roman who complained that India drained Rome of its gold?
Naoroji made the same complaint, the other way round.
He called it the drain of wealth, India's money flowing out to Britain year after year.
But the British also built schools, newspapers, and universities.
And in them, a new generation of Indians learned exactly how to argue with an empire.
One of them was a young lawyer about to be thrown off a train.
